A Suatt Poor—it is an interesting, not to say pretty, sight to watch the under surface of the hart either of a slug or snail in motion, and one which may readily he witnessed by inducing the credure to crawl on a piece of clear glass. A hollow glass cylinder, such as the chimney of a lamp, is preferable to a flat sheet, as affonling greater facilities for close inspection and more ready handling. Having placed the dug, or snail, inside the tube, .ait tin it has got hold with its rocker-like foot, and then turn the gla s round coos to bring the under side into view. So long as the rrriotai remains at rest there is nothing in particular toattract one's attention! hut the moment the creature begins to move a wonderful change takes tolace. The first impression is that 1 there most boa hollow channel along the centre of the foot I through which a (naming torrent it rushing pell-mell from • the tail towards the head. Such, it is scarcely necessary to add, is not the case, and the torrential appearance is solely an optical illusion, due to the successive action of the sur- face of the nauxcular foot in propelling the animal forward. To understand the nature of thiA movement clearly, take I.the cam of a mterpillar when crawling. First the hinder portion of the lowly is drawn up, forming an arch, then the tent in front of the arch are successively raised and those behind set down, causing the arch to move forward towards the head, though the parts of the body maintain the same relative position. fly the time that the first loop, or" wave," in the caterpillar's body has retched its head, which is at once stretched forward, another w wave' has commenced at the tail and to on. Now, the motion in a snail's foot is just the same, only the w way." .lo not affect the whole body, as they do in the caterpillar, and they follow each other so quickly at to give rim to the appearance of flowing liquid. The margins of the foot do not innicipate M this motion, but have gentle, !aural, undulating movement of their own. This motion of the muscular fibres of the foot is under the control of the annum so far as darting and stop ping are concerned ; but the actual motion itself appears to beautomatic, and comparable to that of a locomotive mmine, when the driver turns the steam on or off, leaving the actual work to the mechanism iteelf.—"Ssoils and Sbvs" in Aitner for All" for July. West to AT Newcavn.a li4s.—Pidgeon accompanied Wesley in a tour through the North of England, aml was with him in Newcastle at the note when the oh tbitants of that town were In fear, of an attack from the Pretender's army. The following quaint entry, dated Wednesday, 2:ith I (September, 17t51, purports to have been written in the diary in Neivcastle:—. Our good friends within the walls for ever dinning in our ears, mme, that if we tarry without, the wild Highland men will devour our defeneelem children, and others, that the Orphan House is no placml that so soon as the town guns begin to play, 'twill he levelled with the ground. Mr. Wealey this day made a survey, and he enures me that, on the other hand, the guns are no planted that not a ball can strike on, whilst the lire front New-gate on the one side, and that front Pilgrinnatreet-gate on the other, would blow to faeces any who attempted to come nigh our house to do us harm. To-day he told me somewhat of his former visits to Newcastle. 'llie colliers round about seem to be little less wild than the Scots, their children running half naked, and the men, to show their approval of Mr. ft m. lev, shooting aloud in the midst of the preaching and clap- ping him on the back until hie breath was welbuigh gone. Bat the Newcastle mob, he says, bath somas humanity left at its wildmt. Once, bring moved with compassion for the peer creatures who tient as many still spend) their &In bath in wanderia,7 about the Sandhill, like sheep having no shepherd, he went straight to them from church and started a psalm. 'Fhousands soon gathered round him, but the most part spent the time in ehouting and pushing ; the throng heaving :and towing like a troubletl era. So after singing and praying for art hour in the midst of the tumult, he was constraints', through lack of voice, to leave them without a sermon. Neverthelms, not a stone, brick-hat, rotten egg, or dead cat was thrown, nor was any other per- , sunal violence offered to him. On another occasion, duriag ' his man in the town, the Edinburgh Company of Comedians announced the performance of a farce entitled Trick upon ' Trick, or Methaliein Displayed. A multitude of men and . women amembled to witness the performance, hut, in the first act of the comedy before the farce all the seats erected on the stage gave way with a sudden crack, and dame who eat upon them were throvrn headlong. The play still con- tinuing, after order had been restored, in the wood act all the shilling mats sank suddenly. This mused panic, and many forced their way out of the building in ftst•ror." But still the play went on, When lo! at the *finning of the . dried act, the stage itself went down six inch., the actors skipping nimbly off it in their fright. But having been pursuaded by their master to return, and the piece going on, towanls the end of the third nct all the sixpenny seats fell without the least warning to the ground, and with loud out- cries many more rushed out. Then he who was to play the Methodist, fearing that none would be left to witness his terformance, came lorw.,rd and affirmed that, notwithstand- ing all that had happ(ned, the farce would be performed. As he spake, the stage sank sia inches more, and actors and audience tied in wild confusion "—Passages from the Diary Clans Earie Methatlig. Ity Oulu, &chard Boat.

GROWING 01. b.—DO not too hardily blame the person who in that moment when the concur-taker suddenly pounces upon bis or her age hesitates and prevaricates. Perhaps it is not no much that we do not wish that others should know our ogee as that we do not viisb to confcm to ourselves that we are growing old. And even this is oot a mear and contemptible feeling. The maid of thirty freluently has all the gush and glamour of the girl of sixteen ; and she cannot understand why her age should be in the Roy of eating green apples. Oaring hide-and-seek, cod effecting practical jokea. Sometime; the old girls are the sweemt and cheeriest: and do not men of sixty sometimes think of their selves as the " old girls?" Have you, stripling of twenty,neverroof a grey-haired lout winsome and cheerful lady of fifty to " play up sweet " to? tin find one. She feels an if she were twenty. Ilearts do not grow old—unless they are mean. At least, like good wine, they improve with age.— American Popo.. TAKINO THE CENSCH—The censes has its lighter and more humorous aspects. Another census is blamed fff in" iAg disclosed the foot that in filling up the papers the greater number of lbw who made mistakes were educated people, arid that of all educated blunderers the most incor- rigible were the clergy. The coming returns might also informa to the relative predominance of the Jonmes, Smiths, Browne, and Robinsons,and it might tell on whether any one of these prolific clans has gained ground on any other. As yet it is understood, cuutrary to the general be- lief, that the Joneses are more numerous thin the Smiths, and that after the latter come the byte of Williams,Teylor, Denim, and Brown. Then we shall propably get from the census officers a fresh collection of eccentric uarner, thuugh no. toerhaps .Ider, than that which one registrar has prmerved for the delecta- tion of the curious, to not, Zephitallipmneah Deepen, by trade a cooper, if I remember rightly. The euumerators IBM nary be eble to find out whether Alberti. Regina Cie• toria Gotha Boelt,snother census celebrity, if married, has preserved her extraordinary appellation os'a bort of heirloom in her family, or if P/i“e Albert Daniel I lamon, an agricul- tural labourer whole—Mired ho former returns, has not yet gone over to the majority. We that perhaps discover too if that other labourer who named his daughter Turneries, Henri. Ulrica do Gloria de Lai loin Heti,. Tamer has further developed his marvellous power of appellative com- bination ; or if the father of Hoetilinia Ophiginia Maria Hypihile Wadge hoe christened another daughter with an- centuated eccentricity. In fact, the next censue will, among other things, inform us how for the English people preserve their reputation for oddity, 3 not mimpfftant fact. For, rightly considered, eccentricity is merely a phase of that sturitiMn individualism, that dogged independenm of charm- tee, which, in all ages and all clinics, has made Englishmen a little self-assertive, it may be, but still ever victorious as pioneers of civilised enterpriee and adventure.

dlfElileaX Annterurtng.—The report of Mr. Clare Read and Mr. Pell, the gentlemen sent by the Royal Agricultural Comtnimion to the United States awl Canmla to inquire into the state of agriculture there, hae been published. It comprises If closely-printed folio pagm. 'The Commiseionme conclude by saying that they had not t time for mllecting all the factathey should like to have oh- ' tained; but Morn the information they have got they have arrived at the opinion that after all America it no paradise, that in the contest fur agricultural supremacy, while fresh soil, a level surface, and the absence of stutnee are highly favourable for the profitable use of modern machinery, still I drawbacks exhit which tell in favour uf the old country. Thew may be stated in a few words—severe win.e, putting o stop to agricultural employment, dangerous droughts, in- jurious insects, and in the prairie land, in the absence of lakm, a rhort supply of mod water. With respect to cattle, they my the American stockman in the West M poss, seed of singular advantages, land for nothing, and abundance oft: in the East, good markets for dairy and other values; and in the middle States, excellent pastures ot blue grass. The growth of this plant is extending for beyond its old home— Kentucky—and is now being estwhliehed in the west of Mis- souri. It success opens fresh prospects for the grazier, and will in time bring the improved turf under the hoof of thoroughbrml stock, or at Imat of the highly-graded cattle. The western country is poorly or bred for hotter doses of stock. The allotment of land and the termination of free range will tend to make cattle raising more costly, while, on the other hod, the increased conaumption of the population aa it advances towards the wet.tern plains will enhance prices. _

AID RE TIII:NDERSTOP MS AND FLO3DS• LITRROOOI..—An extraordinary thunderstorm broke with startling suddenness over the city on Saturday night, shortly before ten o'clock. About nine o'clock brilliant flashes of sheet lightning illumined the etreete with remarkable rapidity. Drops of rain after wards began to descend, and about a quarter to ten o'clock a perfect deluge of rain came down. A few minutes before ten a tremendouti thunderclap burst over the city. Several thunderbolts descended in the neighbourhood, and the utmost consternation was created amongst pedestrians who were either in thoroughfare. or were skeltering. The first bolt struck 9, Chester-sr, in the occupation of Mr. S. Jacobs, a loge chimney stack being partly demolished. Two of the errs wore carried away, and the bolt striking the stack horixotitally, solid lumps of brick and stone were hurled into the house, the roomiest,' which , were covered with the delwis and soot. About the arms time two houses, 20 and 22, Beaurnont-st., oecupierl by Mrs. I'. Furness and Mrs. E. Beckett respeetively, were struck be lightning. which entered the bedroom through the roof and splintered the woodwork. No person was Injured. A sad fatality resulted from the startling suddenness and intensity ! of the storm. Mn. W. Hellion, watchmaker, of 55, Park-road, who had been indisposed for some days, retired to rest about ten o'clock, and after the storm broke out he broke a blood vesael and died. A doctor was quickly sent for, and said the deceased had broken the blood vessel in consequence of fright. Puguron.—on Saturday night, about 10-30, a thunder- storm of great severity broke over Preston and the neigh- bourhood, and continued until nearly four o'clock the next morning. Shortly alter the storm began a fatal accident happened to Mr. Joseph Marigold, manager of the lquenix Foundry, in Derby-street, l'reston. Ile and Mr. Thomas Eccles, cashier for 3lessrs. Irvin and Seller., were returning from Blackburn in a trap, drawn by a rather spirited horse, when theanimal took fright at a flash of lightning and bolted. It brought the vehicle in violent contact with some obstacle on the roadside, and it was anashed to mere fragments, the two men being hurled to the ground. Marigold's skull was fractured, and he was killed on the spot. Nista:sly was con- vened tout inn. Eccles was also very severely injured. Waßlitell. —On Saturday night last, about ninw o'clock, the town of Wrexham was visited hy one of the most sever thunderstorms which has ever been known. The were heavy rainfall 'raised the level of the brooks and river, very suddenly, and four bridges, some of large rice, have been washed away by the swollen streams. The damage done to the hay crops is considerable. The low-lying meadows near the Dee are completely aunniertred. MURDER OF MADAME SKOBELEFF.

CON9TANTINOP., Tuesday. Madam Skobeleff, the mother of the well known Rumian general, was murdered on Sunday last, while driving near Thillippopolis, by a Russian sub-lieutenant named Ouisoff, and Nur accomplices, who are stated to be Montenegrins. Tie coachman was also murdered, and an alto-do-camp of General Skobeleff, who was accom- panying the unfortunaM lady e the time, was wounded. The latter, however, succeeded in reaching Phillippopolis, , where heat once denounced Ousg.ff, with whom he was well acquainted, as the assassin had been a frequent visitor at Mglame Skobelefts house. Oussoff, on finding himself in danger. lied to the neighbouring mountains, but was soon captured by a body of cavalry which woe sent in pursuit. He has since committed suicide. The Montenegrins who are accused of being his accomplicea arP in the hands of the police, and his brother, with several of his personal friends, have also been arrested. Robbery is suppose" to have been the motive of the crime, as Madame SkobelefTs money and personal ornamonM were not to be found when the police arrived at the scene of the murders.

MINES IN THIS DISTRICI% Mr. fall, inspector of mines for the Liverpool district, which comprise. West Lancashire and North Wales, in a report recently issued states that 421 eeparate accidents liave been reported during the year 1879, and them have resulted in the death of 97 persons and injury more or leas serious to 345 others. The separate fatal accidents have reached 87, as against 102 in the previous year. The deaths this year ere 207 less than last year, ant are 37 per cent, less then the average for the last six years, during which period the pre- sent act of Parliament has been inoperative. The non-fatal injuries show a decrease of ten. The quantity of mineral raised during the year amounted to 11,875,810 etatuto tors, an increase of 106,244 tons as compared with 1878. The number of persons employed in and about the mines during the year tear been 39,458, as against 39,024 ill 1878, an in- . crease of 434. West Lancashire hag employed 99,354 and North Wales 10,142. The quantity of mineral raised per each person employed in West Lancashire equals 326 tons, and in North Wale; L 96 tons. This apparent difference in individual efficiency appears from year to year, and iris difficult to In the cause. The Youteput "at many of the North Wales collieries is very entail, and machinery for hauling is not so general as in other die- triers, than entailing more manual labour. Lan- cashire and North Wales ere far behind most of the other mining districts of the kingdom as regards immunity from accidents; this is, no doubt, due to some extent to the great depth at which the mines have to be worked and the brittle nature of the shales forming the roofs of the mines, but there ar also otrer GYMS at work. The North Wales portion ef the district holds the unenviable poaition of pre- eenting the highest death-rate in proportion to the quantity of coal raised during the last seven years of the whole of he mining districts of the United Kingdom, with the ex- ceptionof Monmouthshire, end it is far from being naturally the most dangerous. I believe this is greatly due to the managers neglecting to enforce discipline among the work. men, which they are empowered ant required to enforce by the special rules There ere 47 deaths to report under [lie head of falls of roof and side, seven fewer than last year. The onion of Lancashire are very deep, and the strata are often of a very brittls nature, causing a great crush to take place when the coal is removed. This circumstance makes the disWict more liable to Inset accidents front falls of roof and side than others. Many of these accidents from "falls " ariee through "slip." it UR roof, which are difficult to detect and guard against. lea mine liable to these "clips' systematic timbering should be resorted to: that is, timber should be placed at fixed intervala without reference to the appearance of the roof, and at all dangerous points additional timber used. Fifteen deaths have been due to accidents in shafts seven of which were neused by over-winding at the Alexandra pit, the property of the St. Helens Collieries Company, Limited. With reference to the ascot "detaching hooks," Mr. Hall scene--air hat been rowed, that to provide • mmns of safety in cases of over-winding will tend to make enginemen care- lees and inattentive to their work, and so more frequent over- windings will result, and that probably in some of these the epparam wi/I fail to act. Formerly the destruction of pro- perty entailed by an over-wind war a sufficient gurrentee that the engineman would not emeape puniehment, but with 'detaching hooks' and where no damage ensues his neglect may be Feet with • smile." There are 16 deaths to record under the head of miscellaneous accidents underground. Most of these have occurred in passing the coal from the face to the shaft, the accidents taking place generally on the Inclined parts of the mad, through trams either being let loose by those in charge of them or through tackle breaking. A daily examination is made of all machine, underground, in accordance with the Act of Parliament,but.it is impossible , to detect every flaw. Fourteen deaths have been due to accident, on ttie surface, several of which have been mused through engine-drivers and breaksmen in charge of shunting engines failing to see that the waggon roads were clear be- fore moving their trains. Nearly the whole of the accidents on the Narrate have been brought about by the workmen'si want of care for melt other.

The Arvhdesum read the following addrtss to the clergy —lf the histerie lines of the English Church were to be fol- lowed, um of the first act. entailed by the creation of the one Of Liverpool was the formation of an additional ar,ll- - The title of Warrington is new, but the name Itself is that -I one of the olden of our parishm, inscribed in Doomsday Boa, and latterly honourable and generally known to local churchmen as associated with thme ad- mirable institutions which educate the ch,hlren of our clergy nod render help in the duty of trial to their idows aud , Orphan, It has fallen to my lot--and very highly,reverand , kethren, do I esteem the privilege—to lad you welcomer when for the first time as the remora vicar, ang perpetual wit curates hin the limits of the archdeloonry of Warrington you are gathered togefhrr for synodal purporws—to alectpro ors your representatives la the chapterhorme of lock on 11,1 .ttt,,fh.Anulustr. ilena4utl:eun,yano,rl And, „tno_ vocation ehall demand. expressed that con.ocarioansrTnsii7 O rrit."'l"d'rero::til:oo''-ch"11:111Fre!"1 iOgluti"%sep;;:"l.l'llh.nP:od'6",;glliiTrtlfer smart leader writing alone are probably finds con- description of convocation as a pasties. -• It ig genial occupation for episcopal and clerical leisure. to be feared, flowerer, that there ore many staunch friends. among our laymen who have no clear idea aa to the impor- tance of convocation, and who, looking upon it ton kind of effete ecclesiastical organisation, will feel surprise at the interest the clergy rake in this present election. As, then, this ignorance este., and as happily eyery net in connec- tion with our own diocese finds interest with the general public (without unduly magnifying our office) I may in a few words justify our...meetings. I will not refer to certain . canons where it is laid down that the convocations are the true Church of England by representation: boot suggest a careful perusal of the preface to the 39 articles, where, in the king'. declaration we read u that the O churchmen may do the work which is proper unto ! them, the bishops and clergy from time to time, in convon- don upon their humble Arnie, shall have license ender our broad esel to deliberate of and to do all such thinge as, being made plain to them and assented unto by an. shall concern the settled continuance of the doctrine and discipline of the ' Church of England now eetablished, from whicn we will not endure any varying or departing in the least degree." Frankly acknowledging that we no longer bare power of , separate taxation, and that convocation is strictly. limitsd in its power to make ecclesiastical regulation, Ale here re- , cognised—and we claim that it would be contrary to rea.n and common sense if it were otherwise, that the church. an an ecclesi.tical organisation, has the privilege of meeting in delilmrative assembly. Further, it in noteworthy , that the period of greatest lethargy and apirittial inaction in our English Church history Las the time during which mmalal action was dormant, and when the church was ch mired of that privilege which every other religious body possessed, of discussing her own affairs in her own amenibly. Further. it is well to remember that when in the days oi Charles II the noncentortniats urged • gcnerst religious union by confining the terms of Com- munion to points &mind egnerilial, their propcmile included an elaborate scheme of synodal represetitation—parxhial, ruridecanal, diocesan, and 10r00100io11 for they suggested that all the bishops or superintendent. of the two provinces of Canterbury and York, together with a certain number of the clergy to be elected out of the various eioc,..es. should form a provincial synod or eanvocation, to meet every third ymr, with the primate of each province prceiding inmle- rotor. The relative value of the Convocation of York, as compared witb that of Canterbury, hoe, I cannot but think, been u folly depreciated. The historian, by common consent calk.] impartial, hae ,alt, u The eanvor a- tion of the province of Canterbury. of which alone we nerd meek, for that of 'fork appears never to have been impor- hat ;" and this verdict is ton generally assumed on apply- ing to the 'tweet state of things instead of one now lon< weed. This discredit is due to two cameo, one of which the Convocation of York must share with its sister oonyncm tin of the south. The intolerable wranglinm in connection with the Bangorian controversy supplinl material Intro Lord Mahon) fora large volume, but interest only torn single page. Thom were the days when the oft-repented cry of " The Church in Banger " was a political watchword, not the expression of spiritual anguish, when the only security of the church rimmed to oonsirt in pert/lines, her only remedy a sect. Those were limes of such deplorable deadness to spiritual realities that it was found posail,le for the great satiriet gravely to assert "that he did not think it wholly groundless or Ilia fears altogether imaginary that the abolishing of Christian ity would perhaps bring the church into danger, or at least put Parlia- ment to tile trouble of taming another v.. that the church is in • most safe and nourish- ing condition." Thme were the days when proctors In convocation ,were aelected, not so much for prudence and piety, but because they were political wheelie. Thank God, the safety of the Church of England now lem Oboe ever rests upon a parliamentary vote of confiffiniee. It in because she sets before ber, as first and foremost. the great misaion with which her divine Master Imit invested her, that she lives in the affections of the people, riot dreads no pauic my of the chnrch in danger. With the full conscious.. of all our difficulties and division, let us take courage, and . we elect our proctors thank God that it is not to the Convcca- lion of Queen Aline', but to that of our most gracious Queen Victoria. The other cannot direr,' it has aiso passed away. 11 had its rise in the inaimdfinnce of our northern province. Then the archbishop bad only as suffragans the Bishopsof Burharthearlisle,and Chester, whilst the dioccasan of Mn. was too often separated from :he mainland by strong waters. With the sparse population and miserable means of transit, the visit of proctors to York were like angel. few and far between. Manchester and Leeds were then wall towne with but ,few thousand, whilst Liverpool was still thinking of the days when her largest ship was a barque of 40 tong, with a crew a twelve men, and when all her ships only numbered twelve, her tonnage 233 tona and her sailors 75 men. It W. rna. privilege to appmr for the first tint. fewdays ago in the ehapter.house of York, and to her the primate, supported by some suffragan, with a crowd of proctors, in the lower bow*, and a multitude of anxiou, earnest churchmen, to Eaten to • debate sustained on both shim with such ability and force as may be equalled, but could not be excelled, in the con- vocation of the southern province. The fount then, as to our non-iniportanco, has p.sedaway,and I congratulale my brethren as well as myself that we belong to a province whose convocation is • pattern to that of Canterbury. Amid their rn.y needed reforms they urge, most of all, th,, in Can.rbury, as with on, the bmhops and clergy may AIL to,e- ther and enjoy the advantages of facedo-face with freedom. brit with fairness dischasing the common interests, and of manifmting how liberty of •poech may Immo! without de- generating into license. And further, that Canter- , bury may reeemble York in aa reprmentative ' character. In the south each diocese has only it, two proctors, and thus London, with its 446 benefice, Lincoln with its SOS, and Norwich with its 914, bas but the same amount of representation which we to-day enjoy in our new archdeaconry with its 96 beneficce, where, otter the rule of the north, we, in common with the other arch- deaconries, are to pomeen our two repremontiven. Legal formalities, however, meted always be are,le- , rated, and thankful I am that such has been the 1,101, for I cdnvocation is nothing unless it be fairly representative, and to accomplish thin there ROME not be that which all alike would regret, viz., taking by eurprine. Ic another part of this day's Examiner we pub. huh a report of the proceediogo which took place on Monday during an interview between Earl Spencer the Lord President of the Privy Council), Mr. Mundell., M.P. the Vice. President of the Privy I Council), and a deputation representieg Lead., Sal- I ford, Halifax, Manche•ter, Bureley, Ashton-under. Lytle, Boston, Sheffield, Birmingham, and Peter. borough, a conriderable oprinkling of Lancaohire I members being among the deputation. The chief ; spokesmen were Mr. Jacob Brlitht, M.P., Mr. Brigge, It P., Mx. Arnold, M.P., Mr. Armitage, M.P., the I Mayor of Salford, Mr. Priue, of Mancheoter, Mr. J. Whitehead, of Leeds, and Mr. Mowers, of Birming• ham. Those proceedings will be perused with great , intoest throughout the kiimdion, as the subject die. I cussed is one of Ili tional importance. Flesh meat forma the main and nest enjoyable part of the diet of the Euglish people, and the oupply of whole. some animal food at remimable price.; therefore, a matter of great national counern. Everybody old I enough to remember will recollect the great vigilante that waa deployed by the authorities in 111;7.8.7, when the riederpest woe introduced, as was alleged at the time, by the importation int., this country of Russian cattle. Since then the restrictions . upon the importation of foreign live gook have been gradually drawn tighter ; and the periodical appear. I ance of such distempers as foot and mouth dieoaae, ! I pleure-pneumonia, and miler maladies peculiar to live stock, have revved no onetime, and, probably, justly ao. In 1178, an Act—which was oeverely oon,bated it the time by the Liberals, who were then I in opposition—eulorging and defining the powers of the Privy Council in prohibiting the importatiou of live cattle from abroad, was panted but prior to the posing of that Act the Privy Council had, under existiog nuanced, authority to schedule certain oonntries, and to prohibit all importation of tattle from thaso countries. By the apt of 1878 it was ordained that all foreign cattle arriving in port should be olaughtered in port, except I such as were brought to this country from abroad for , I exhibition or for exceptional purposes. The Privy ICouncil was given executive powers and certain die- , eretionary latitude, so long no the termed the statutes were complied with, in closing the ports agaiuot cattle tram certain countries. In replying to the ; deputation, Earl Spencer mid his Offlee might except, and ohould except, from the.prohibitory order countrire . whore the Privy Council were eatisfied that the laws 1 of the country relating to the importation and expos- ; tation of animal., and to the prevention and spread of disease, were such no to secure general security against disease. Only when the Privy Council were no satisfied they might give order for the admission of . cattle, which after twelve hours' detention might be passed throughout the country. But the importa- tion of cattle from countries where rinderpeat had existed was entirely prohibited. There were It ports where cattle which could be admitted free might be ! landed. There were 15 ports where cattle might be !. bided where they had to be slaughtered. The number of cAintrioa seladuled hod varied at different times. The couotries from which importation was ! prohibited were Austro-Ifungary, Italy, Montenegro, I Russia, Roumania, and Turkey, including the pro. emcee of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The countries that might hi leg in their animalis were Her Majeety's dominions in North America, Denmark, Norway, Sweden, Spain, end Portugal. The Privy Connell had no power if admitting any cattle from any country ueloso they were matisfied that it was a country Lee from diaease. The object of the deputa- tion was to relu,et that these restrictions now Co rigidly applied ebould be slackened, as the deputation and those whom they represented believed them in many instances to be unnecessary, and that they limited the supply of auimal food, affected im quality, and enhanced the price. The:plaino of America have for some yeare now contributed oar chief supply of flesh meat, and Mr. Jacob Bright told the Lord . President of the Privy Council and his colleague that '• there is a very wide and deep feeling ea to the restriction. on American cattle. It was stated that American cattle which came to this country were more healthy on the average than the cattle of the United Kingdom, and it wm held, upon what appeared to him somewhat strong evidence, that the proofs of the diseme of plenee.; pneumonia, which war the reaam why, as be understood, American cattle were not allowed to I come to our towns, were not convincing, in fact, , a belief widely prevailsd that the diseese did not exist in America at all." At present a vast I quantity if desd meat is oupplied from the Staten, ! and by the time it reachea the inland towns of this country, in hot or damp weather, it is ready to perioh. The animals that arrive in port alive are there slaughtured ; our home stock it yearly I on the decreme, and as the population of the cotoitry increasea home producers will find it more and more dif6,ult to keep pace with the demand. The effect of all the, was very fairly put by Mn. The opposition to the Liverpool Water Hill, by the Run- corn Improvement Commissioners, though left h, the last moment, has fortunately 'united 0 their being granted similar, if even not greater privilegen, than have been given to other town, by the Corporation of that city. No one doubts the value of an economical procedure on the part of all public bodies, but there is a false economy, a bastard prudence which tinils favour with sorne individuals, and that aught to he condemned in unmeasured terms by all who have the good of their native town at heart. I doubt not that there are many ratepayers in Widnes who, if they had hal the power, would have prevented any such action as that which the Local Board of that town have taken, but I think any thoughtful loan who has mental cap wity to fore- see what is very likely to happen owing to the continuous growth of the place, Moot admit that it would be a most thsantrous thing fur WWIIre to be hampered in its extension, in say toner twenty years, by 11 WAOI of a sufficient supply of water.

div.p: ATHEISM, dec. • I Sir,—Kindly excuse me for troubling vou with a •ew more word. in answer to Mr, Bennett. Had that gentleman answered my arguments inatead of tweeting that he could, but would sot. poesibly I might have hid my diminished head, or else have declared myeel I • convert to Ins views. All the rubbish about line lashing their tails, ec,, counts for nothing. The fact is, each Bishop's charge circulated amongst the clergy daring the last ten years bemoans 11. e immense arid, that Atheism is making amongst all claws of society, re-re especially the educated. The formation and failure of Christi. Evidence and kindred eocieties speaks with A trumpet voice far above • whale menagerie tall of tail laehings. Mn, 'Sennett, in the course of his gashing letter, rotor. to Heists and Atheista as if the tern., were synonym... •I erhaps it would be as well if hewer, to reek information on this subject in another column et your paper. lie also glows Thomas Paine credit Ice uttering mine foolish words when on his deathbed. Mr. Bennett wins to be in total liteknese on each and every •subject upon which he touches. I have a paper before me, written by T. Paine, entitled "Mr thoughts on a future Ills," in which he saya, I hope for happiness after this life. I consider myself in the bands of my Creator, and that he will disease of me after this life consistently with his juatice and gassiness." Hoes the Unitarian any more or lees th. ,se By the bye. Mr. Bennett seems to refer to the Unitarians in a very tender leaden, and am sure the few who ere "not beyond the range of possibility " will feel much cbliged to Mr. Bennett for the hied offer of • '• better habitation." Mr. Ilennett . acknowledges twdietorted Christianity, ' awl "that outrageous crimes have twit perpetrated end, its shadow," yet in the same breath we are told. the invariabliseffect of Ohristianitv hae been to civilise the barbarous, to encourage science,' le. Why, sir, what are the facm as ra,orded in history? Geography pointato•Columbus and a Magellan. Aetronomy to a Copernicus (with a pereecubar in thc mild Melancliton). to • Roger Boot, and (hill.. The Eyes of these free- thinkers irave the reverse at what Mr. Bennett amens, Civilleing the barbarous! Christianity, throggliJohn Calvin, burned Seryitue and beheaded (tract, and wurdered Bruno. The Christian blood ehed by Pagan pers.:aloes is insignifi- cant when compared with the blood of liereLcs and free- thinkers.shed by Christianity itself. The lansubstantiation controverey coat more than amooo lines, and the famous image controversy 50,000. In Greece alone 100,000 lives were merificed by the permeations instgated in the ninth century against the Manieheans. The fameat schism which preceded the burning of Huss and Jerome cooot in the end 150,040 lines. The extermination of the Albigenses and the expulsion of the Miristmes represent a lose of liwidreda of thousands mote. Add to these the 40,080 livesawiliced in the St. Bartholomew massacre, the 50,000 persona killed in the Netherlands by Charles V., the 31.000 horned to death by the Spanish inquisition, and you will have a record of slaughter in the name of Christianity which throws over, thing elm in the shade. Moncure Conway says "the church killed off all men of ability who would not eubmitto it," and lank in what department of science woe the church aver right? Point out owe country under the rule of the church, amt yon will see a cmuntry lost in ignorance and supersti- tion. In all cogs ignorance seems lobe the mother of de- votion; and it has only been since men evinced a determina- tion to think for themmlves that the church has relaxed its coils. To-day in Warrington, Dissenters, amongst wham I class Unitarians,dare not allow Mr. Braollaugh, M.P., or Mn,. Flemnt, to lecture in the Co-operative Hall to-day the directors of the Public Hall dare not let that building for a lecture, fear leet the young mind should be taught to strike out into deep water, independent of theological blad- der. who have " had enough of Mr. Bradlaugh." Gently, my friend, you areonly at the conimencement of your troubles. C. Bradlaugh is like one crying in the wilderness to prepare the way. He is but the forerunner to a hoet of determined men, who will make it pnesible for Itifillmen to live in Ire- land. whn will tell the English landlord to mend his ways, or else clear out bag and loggage ; men who care more for their fellow countrymen and women than they do for hares and rabbits, men who will carryout that old injunction, °He that will not work et ther shaft he eat." Who will stop rich brewers from cursing a town with gin shop, and paving thed own way to heaven be building churches. Mr, Ben- nett may sneer at Mr. Gladstone ; it will be as effective as Mrs. Partingtoc4 mop. Honesty an truth must make head- way in spite ofill the Christian juggernauts that may try te block the way. If Mr. Bennett will read White's Warfare of Science lie will not betray SUCiI deplorable ignorance next time be tries to defend Christianity.—Yours, IL WIIITIIAM.

TtiE routmos OF THE 61ERSEY. Sir,—l have a complaint to make. I have wrenched several buttons off the calm of several of my acquaintance. in vain attempts to detain them while I told my weary tale. Into you attentive ears I must pour the burden of nip sorrows, it most patient of editors! And I ate the more em- boldened in this inaannich an they are not merely aeldsh sorrows, but are shared more or lee,' be my fellow townsmen, viz., I and my friend P. B, by the land permission of the owner, took a flight in the Womlcock front Warrington Bridge to Illoylake and Hilbre Island. But it is not so much about this part of our trip that I shall trouble you. Suffice it to say that we were both well pleased with things as we found them beneath the wood-girt shores of Etstham, where we spent a day and two nights, or at New Brighton, upon the ever-heaving water. of which we spent one night, to be awakened in the morning imy a fog-horn reeriVe, the weather being very thick and hazy,necessitatieg the frequent use by the inward-hound ocean steamers of these hoarse-toned announcements of each other's whereabouts. The timle wan at its height, and to those like ourselves, outward bonnd, it was time to he on the move. So beneath time white walls of the New Brighton Pharos, the Rock Liglithome, we stole through the thick air of that early morning into the Rock Channel, where we overtook other vessels, like our selves drifting westward on the slowly ebbing tide waiting and wishing for a wind. Thin came at last, and wafted or to our destination in Iloylake. This was on the ammo.] of gajory,i lasz Jr tfie evening we again spread the wingn of tke Woodcock, and had a frptn through the dark green waters to Hilbre Island. Now, to people fMIO this was a treat. Used as we are to sailing in what at beet is only liquified mud, and that of a quality not pleasant Indwell upon in any sense of the word, we thoroughly ap- preciated the change to water where you might see the hot- torn long before you grounded upon it, and where, when the sun shine., you man see the various forum of marine animal life disturbed in their retreats by the passage of the boat. As the shades of evening clean!, and the wind fell, promis- ing a repetition of the morning fog, we sought a convenient resting place near the entrance of the lake. Saturday night first will long be remembered by many for its thunder and lightning. We had our chars of it but that is not what I complain about. The sight wee awfully and beautifully grand. The frequent brilliancy of the Bashes illumined sea and the coast, render- ing objectr thereon as distinctly visible as in broad daylight. The morning broke with a One breeze from the west, before which we scudded over the long rolling swells up the Rock Cimnnel, past New Brighton. Liverpool, and into Tranmere Bight. where, to the accompaniment of the whistling wind, and 311111 pelfing showers, we dined. From thence, being A favouring gale, we sped past Garston and Pungeon to Runcorn, whore we found the upper Mersey in flood after the rain., and conse- quently our chances of reaching Warrington very poor indeed as the wind had gradualiT fallen away and at last Alnweteotirrly left us. Be a diligent use oi the oar we forced the boat through floe turbid waters to the "Old Handle," where we passed our fifth night. But what a con- trast this, in surroundings, to our fourth night. Then we had the pure salt-Laden breezes charged with health-giving zone, and in the intervals of the thunder, the lullaby of Bell Buoy as it rocked upon the surge. Here we were half poisoned by feted effluvium arising from the water on which we bad to spend the night. It was foul to every sense. It of 7 ended the eye by its greasy blackness and the nainelesa abominations it bore upon ile reeking bosom as it stole by unlike a guilty thing too foul and greasy to be tickled into a rippling Inugh by the toying of the wind playing on its surface. In sober earnestness, Mr. Editor. we were coin- pelletl to sleep upon the out.poutings of the sewers of Manchester, Salford, in, to say nothing of the contribu- tions of our own town. Now, air, I remember a place down in Howley they had used to call the honey pot. It was merely an open sewer where the rejectinenta of the town were allowed Co fester in the sun. Ws are. happily, rid of that nuisance. Now my complaint is, and I commend Otto the consideration of our Town Council, especially to those members of it who are interested in our noble river, that we folks in Warrington should be compelled to dwell upon the banks of what is, practically, nothing more titan an open sewer, which conveys past mar very doors the offensive out- owning. of an immense population. I said conveyed, hut, unfortunately, all of it is not conveyed away. Warrington ie the head if the tidal syetem of the upper Mersey, and here the sewage.chargett waters are checked by the tides and discharge a large proportion of their filthy burden on the backs, where it is left to reek and fester in the sun. Now, sir, is it not a disgrace to our mmdern civilisation to allow euch aerate of things to cola? Can modern engineering denier on way for the destruction or wde and inoffensivel conveyance of Ohms matters past our doors? The time wil come when the population of the Mersey basin will need to combine and coostruet a main drab, independent of the river. It is the height col barbarism to thus destroy the beauty and utility of one of nature's most beautiful constructions. —I ani, do, JOHN PREIts. Warrington, July 19,1680.

div.p: WARRINGTON-NEW MARKET. DEPUTATION OF SHOPKEEPERS TO THE MARKET

The dissahsfaction with the new market arrangements which, at the last meeting of the Council, Councillor Dixon said existed in the town, on Tuesday took a practied shape. On that day a &potation of shopkeepers in the vicinity of the Market Hall waited upon the Market Committee to present a petition in reference to the alterations. The deputa- tion consisted of Mr. William Sharp, Mr. Jchn White, Mr. Milling, Mr. W. Dutton, fir. P. Leigh, Mr. John Cross, Mr. It. L. Pierpolnt, Mr. J. Galloway, and Mr. J. M'Collom. There was a fair attendance of the members of the Council, sad Om chair was occdplod by Alderwau Masflekt Mr. &iamb in Introducing the depuut Ina, presented the petition, which he said was signed by ItIP persons, chiefly tradespeople, whose place of busineas was near the rad market, and who felt that an injustice was done to them by the removal of the principal portion of the market neople into the new huilnting. The diversion of traffic which had taken place was of such a serious nature that in same abatis now en a market day they did nod take as tnanv shillings as they used to take pounds. People had taken Lang lease, of shops in the vicinity of the old masket, never dreaming of any such alteration an hot now beeu made, and they would con- sc quently las great sufferers from the change. The crowded state of the thoroughfares in the old market, which, it tens admitted, called for some alteration, weak! have been met by simply removing the drapery and crockery stalls to the new market, and leaving, the rdied adjoining the Market Hall exclusively for greengrocers and country salespeople, the latter of wham equally objected to the change of position. NIL Jons tbttroc, w Ito appeared for one of the largest owners of property up to the old market—Colonel Bieck- borne—and at the roquest of his tenants, said that when many years ag,o the Late Mr. Blacklmrne sold his interest in the market tolls to the Corporation for a nominal sum, it was certainly never expected that this alteration of the posi- tion of the nt trket would be made, end that his successors should suffer inconsequence. While perfectly aware that private interests must give way to the public convenience, he contended that the new arrangement was not a public convenience, but rather the contrary, and was ca'culated to drive away greengrocer. rather than to encourage them. Mr. NIILLING 'Laid his premise. were seriously deteriorated in the selling value by the change. Ile thought that the butter people ought to be brought back Mto the Market Hall, I the and entirely reserved for green grocers, who ought to be encouraged in every way, and the drapers' stalls pat all together in the new market Mr. Derrow said lb it a great injustice was being done to the drapers by the encouragement of those small drapers, who had no rates or taxes to parr, ant only a small toll instead of tent. It war inmossible that the drapers of the town could compete with them under press, eiretunatances, nor was it fairthat the shopkeepers should be placed in such a position. These a rag merchants" took away out of the town iSHO or £l,OOO each week, which wan a serious nutter and must be against the interests of the town generally. The other members of die deputation having spoken, Tbe CHAIRMAN mid he regretted that the deputation had not come some time ago. The committee had beard a goal deal that was new to them, and which together with the petition should be fully considered. The committee had already decided that some moditication of the new arrange- ment most be made, but what alteration would be made he could not at present say. Although it wasadifficult mstter to pleaee everyone. the deputation might bo armored, that in I all the committee did they bad simply the welfare of the town and ratepayers at heart. IThe deputation then withdrew.

The members of the Loyal Stonehenge Lodge celebrated their anniversary on Monday. A procession was formed at the London Bridge inn, at nine o'clock, and headed by the Statham brass band marched through the village, calling at the resiihnees of the principal residents. The procession afterwards attended St. Thomas's church, where service was conducted and a special sermon preached by the Rev. T. , Greendl, vicar. At the conclusion of the service the mem- bers again formed themselves in. procergion and visited the residences of several other gentlemen, after which they returned to the clubhouse, where a capital dinner was pro- vided, between sixty and seventy members being present. After dinner the Vice, presided and was simported by Noble Grand Arch George Parr (vice-chairman), the District Master bow. Ritteraby, Vice District Master Daniel Dean, Alfred Few (secretary of the Stonehenge Lodge), Charles Beech (treasurer), Andrews, .d William Worsley. Letters of apology were read from the member lee the borough. Mr. John Gordon McMinnies, M.P., Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., Mr. Robert Davies, Mr. Peter Whitley, Sc. The usual loyal toast haring been honoured, Mr. G.. PARR proposed " The Bishop and Clergy of the Diocese, and the Ministers of all denominations."

--T;'i:7;i1;;;;;Is;id—hT;;;;;;;:e the bishop and all minis. tern had sympathy with friendly societies. The objects of friendly societies called forth the sympathies of oilmen who , really cared for their fellow-men. He only wished every- I body belonged too club of soine bird, and that they codes- voured Co provide for a rainy day. Sickness was had in it- self, but it was very bad when combined with poverty. Mr. FEW proposed .` The Warrington District Order of Druids," and spoke of the present proeperous condition of the Order in the district, which numbered about 1,300 mom. bare. _ .

Mr. dauss BAITERSIIIi,IiiSWitt 'luster, responded and said that daring his term of office the laws of the Order in the district had been revised, and they heped to present laws for the district of which they need not be ashamed. A , point which all friendly soeeties had neglected WAS WI !see that old men who were past work were properly looked after. In their society as in ml other friendly societies, they only allowed old men past work half-a-crown a week super- annuation allowance; but although they only received hall• a-crown per week they were subject to the some rules as members who were simply upon the society for a short time owing to sickness. The, thought that war not right, and they believed that old men who were no longer able to fol. , low their employment shonld be cared for by the society. which should see that their old age was made comfortible. To eff,ct that purpose they vreregoing to form a fund called the superannuation fund, to establish which each member would be levied a very small amount per quarter. From that fond old members wlmm they knew to be past meek would be provided for, and would not htve to go to the workhouse, as some of the members had to do.

BAD MEAT IN THE WAIIIIINOTON MAD...T.—John Back-1 houae, butcher. Market-hall, wan charged with baying in hi.l possession, on the loth of July inst , certain niece, to wit 159 pieces of beef, intended for human food, which were then diseased and unwholesome, and unlit for human food. Mr. Davies appeared. on behalf of the town clerk, to prosecute, and Mr. Moore, in the absence of Mr. Cattingham. defended. Inspector Hinman said he went to the defendant's shop on the 10th not.. and thtre saw, and exa,nined, the meat in question. and finding it unsound had it conveyed to the Town Hall. The meat was, in his opinion, eanoeed for sale. —Hr. Joseph said that he examined the meat and found it wholly unfit for human foal. The flesh of the animal mist have been unhealthy when it was killed. It had been suffer- ing from "grapes," kind of consumption, and, according to the latest authority on floe subject, any human beings eating the meat would he liable to be .1,4 with the same disease.--Mr. Prof. Well KAM he had examined the pieces of meat in question ow the 10th July,and found the whole to be portion of an animal that hail dint in the last etage of pthimis. pulmonalia, or grape. The pieces were wet, sticky, and flabby. and very much dixolourwl and in his opinion the whole lot was uufit for the food of man.—Mr. Moore, for the defence, said he was sorry he could not bring Mn. Bennett, of Much Hall farm, from Irlwan the defendant bought the animal for £l3 10s, there to testify that when he sold the cow it was, Co far as he knew,ia a perfectly sound condition, and when a man et Mr. Bennett's experience could he deceived how much store easily would it he for • man like defendant.—A witness was examined for the defence who said that the cow wae purchased on Wednesday and that to all appearance it was a healthy animal.—The magistrates retired for consultation, and on their return the Mayor said that the case was a very grave one indeed, and the magis- trates were resolved to put down such practices. It was de- plorable to think of the meat being sold f rom Wednesday toll Saturday.—The defendant WA. fined £.lO, the alternative being three months' imprisonment. The fine was paid. At that time their charges were £1,533,000, and he proposed to raise £1,914,000, which would leare surplus of £381,900. On the other side they had to most supplemental estimates of £OOO,OOO. The noble lord (Lord G. Hamilton) contended that those ought to be met out of the awing", of the year. That was a proposition which might not unfairly be made with regard to supplemental estimates coming at the end of the financial year; but he pointed out that these were made early in the r creel year, or he might say in the last quarter tif the last year, and they were estimates for which the late Government were reeponsible rather than the present. He had taken the charge for changing the malt duty at no more than £1,100,000 out since that time investigations hail been made which showed that some not inconsiderable changes were necessary. One change—a very costly one, though apparently insignificant—was the alteration of the scale or specific gravity from .55 to .57, which would cost for the five months of the year not left than £230,000, end already £50,000 had been added to that charge. But on the other hand they might gain £233,000 in respect of the wine duties, and the result was that there was only £.53.000 that he w-as aware of thai tended to vary the balance he gave to the House. The income I,IX of course stood as it did, and with respect te the licenses there was no inaterial change, so that on the crelitor side they had £1,914,000, and 011 the debtor side 21,420,000. leaving a surplus tif £434,000, which he did not think an unreasonable one. The and of it was that they adhered to those estimates of revenue, and they could not, as tiersons responsible to the State and the couniry, with prudence or propriety alter them. He had been surprisi,d that bon members on the opposite side who were so shocked at the increase of a penny to the income tax bad never been shocked when increases were made for the purpose of plungitg into fearful and un- fathomable gel fs of expenditure. (Hear, hear.) He disliked all augmentations of the income tax, but he would say this, that if it were to be augmented, the time when they might view that augnienMtion with satisfaction was when it woe made for the purpose of liberating the industry of the country. A revision ..-iorarnittee having been appointed by Of tinardians to go through the several dis- tricts end enquire into the circumstanceo of individuals receiving relief, their object being to see that the poor are properly attended to, and whelSar any taring of the rate he effected. Fizz or aWlexerrort COLLIZIti.—NARaow FACAPR or COLLIBIIB.—The fire which broke out in the pit belong tag to the Halsnead Colliery Co., Whist., mill remains are extinguished, all the efforts, of the managers having proval futile. On Monday morning a violent explosion occursed In the No. 2 Pit from the result of the tire, and a large lum- ber of people assembled at the pit mouth, fearing that a loss of life had taken place. The men, however, had a narrow escape, for, fortunately, they were quietly getting their breakfasts above when the explosion occurred. There is no doubt that had they been in the pit when the explJosion oc- curred, a lose of We would have ensued. The ff.. seerne to he gaining ground, and the officials of the colliery are in despair as to what steps to take to prevent the spread of the subterraneons conflagration. FATAL COLLIERY AOCITALTT AT Si. HELENS. Ant inquest was held on Tuesday last at the Royal Oak, Parr, before C. E. Driffield Es:, Coroner, on the body of John Orrell, aged 29, collier, living at Parr. It appeared from the evidence that the deceaswl was engaged as • - tunk rider" at the Havannah pit belonging to Messrs. Evans and Co. in Tharsday last the 16th inst. he went to work as usual about 8 p.m., and about half pun two was proceeding with a num- ber of waggons of coal to the top of the 'crow," he sitting °ti- the top of the first waggon. As the trucks did not arrive at the end of their journey in time, a night fireman named Tatiana went to see what was the muse of the delay, when he found the deceased with his head jammed between the roof and the waggon. When liberated he was found to be quite dead. The jury retarned a version of "accidental death." BATRINO FLTurnt AT ST. Har..nrs.—An inquest was held on Tuesday lent, at the Prince. Royal Notch Park-road, St. Helens, before Mr. Harker, deputy coroner, on the body of Ernest Lawton, aged 12 years, the son of John Lawton, of the Old Locks, Parr, who was drowned the previous Saturday afternoon by bathing in the Sankey canal. It appeared that the !al left home on the Saturday pre:ions about halt-pact ter t, go and pick coal on • rail- way siditi, and for the par p .-, h lying a bithe. He intended bathing id a brook close by It canal, but flatting it dry. imprudently went to bath, hi the ooa.l A man named Roberts saw the hid Lubin., in V..e caual about 12 o'clock, and a lad standing on the Lank watching him. When Roberts Lad got ation:lo9 yards away he turned round and saw the lad gesticulating laudly tail for help. He went back as fast as he could, and found the lad drownin,g. He was sinking for the third time when he got there. He Tea no swimmer, no lie dare not venture in, althongh or A.lti at the i,neat the w'mar ooly stout tone feet doer, rtr, tot Bradley. hownner, tO' OF, shortly after, and the lifeless body of the la.d was taken from tha canal. The jury returned a verdict of "ACcident .lly drowned whilst bathing.'
